strengths: Identifies and formalizes an underexplored and practically relevant problem (Noise-Aware Generalization) at the intersection of Domain Generalization and Learning with Noisy Labels, supported by clear motivating illustrations (Fig. 1, Fig. 3).

Provides a genuinely useful contribution to the community by manually annotating label noise in VLCS and analyzing noise structure in CHAMMI-CP, which could serve as new benchmarks for this line of work.

Extensive empirical comparison spanning 11 SOTA DG/LNL baselines and 18 combination variants across two real-world and two synthetic-noise datasets, with useful discussion of failure modes of naive LNL+DG combinations (e.g., domain-distribution skew from sample selection).

The core idea of using cross-domain feature comparisons (rather than within-domain distance/loss) to disambiguate label noise from domain shift is intuitive, simple to implement, and plug-and-play with existing DG pipelines.
Additional analyses (e.g., quality vs. quantity trade-off in sample selection, ranking reversals of LNL methods when combined with DG) offer some useful insight for future work in this space.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is essentially a restatement of Assumption 1 under an expectation over other domains, not an independently proven result; no derivation or proof is given, undermining its status as a 'theorem' and the claimed theoretical grounding of the method.

The proposed solution assumes access to domain labels, which is acknowledged as a limitation of the 'naive' baseline but DL4ND still requires this same information; the paper does not adequately address settings where domain labels are unavailable or noisy themselves.

Results are inconsistent: in Table 3, ERM+++DL4ND sometimes shows a performance decline (e.g., -2.5% ID accuracy at 0.2 noise on OfficeHome), and in Table 2 DL4ND+DG gains over the best DG/LNL baselines are often marginal (e.g., CHAMMI-CP OOD, ID accuracy is sometimes lower than plain LNL methods), weakening the claim of consistent improvement.

The paper explicitly cites Qiao & Low (ICLR 2024) as the closest prior work analyzing noise-robustness in DG (and even uses it to motivate Fig. 1), yet never includes it as an experimental baseline for direct comparison, leaving the central novelty claim only partially substantiated.

No reported variance/multiple-run statistics across the many experiments (18 combination methods x multiple datasets), making it difficult to assess whether the reported gains are statistically meaningful versus noise in single-run comparisons.

The technical novelty of DL4ND is somewhat incremental: it combines standard GMM-based loss splitting (as in DivideMix-style methods) with (class, domain) prototype-based relabeling, which is a relatively straightforward extension of existing sample-selection LNL ideas to the multi-domain setting.

Presentation has rough edges (e.g., typo 'Compairisons' in a section title, dense notation, some claims like '20% relative gain' are not easy to directly trace to specific table entries), reducing clarity and reproducibility for readers trying to verify specific numeric claims.

strengths: Identifies and formalizes a practically important, underexplored intersection of Domain Generalization (DG) and Learning with Noisy Labels (LNL), which the paper terms Noise-Aware Generalization (NAG); this framing is well motivated by real-world scenarios (web-scraped datasets, biological imaging).

The RotatedMNIST toy analysis (Sec. 3.2, Fig. 3) provides a clear and intuitive illustration of why noisy samples and domain-shifted samples can be confused by standard distance/loss-based criteria, giving good intuition for the proposed solution.

Effort to curate/annotate real-world noise in VLCS and to leverage CHAMMI-CP as noisy multi-domain benchmarks is a useful contribution to the community, going beyond purely synthetic noise evaluation common in prior work.

Reasonably extensive empirical comparison, spanning 11 baseline DG/LNL methods and 18 combinations across two real and two synthetic noisy datasets, with pseudocode provided for reproducibility of the integrated baselines.

The proposed DL4ND mechanism (using low-loss samples as per-domain-class proxies and cross-domain distance comparison for relabeling) is a simple, plug-and-play idea that is easy to integrate into existing DG pipelines.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is not actually proved anywhere in the paper; it is simply restated from Assumption 1 (itself an unproven existence assumption) with domain index changed. Presenting this as a "Theorem" without any derivation or proof sketch is misleading and overstates the theoretical rigor of the contribution.

Empirical results are mixed rather than uniformly positive: on CHAMMI-CP, several DL4ND+DG combinations actually show lower ID accuracy than baseline ERM or DG-only methods (e.g., MIRO+DL4ND ID 70.38 vs. ERM baseline 77.07), and in Table 3, ERM+++DL4ND shows a decline at 0 noise-level comparisons (-2.5%, -0.6%), undermining the claim of consistent improvement.

No error bars, variance, or multiple-seed results are reported anywhere in the main results tables (Tables 1–3), making it impossible to assess whether the reported gains (including the headline "up to 20% relative gain") are statistically significant or within run-to-run noise.

The real-world evaluation is limited to only two datasets (VLCS, CHAMMI-CP), which is a fairly narrow empirical base for a paper proposing a new task and claiming general applicability across "diverse fields"; the other two datasets used are synthetically noised versions of standard DG benchmarks, not independent real-world noise sources.

The core technical novelty is relatively incremental: constructing class/domain prototypes from low-loss samples and relabeling by nearest cross-domain prototype closely resembles existing similarity/cluster-based LNL sample-selection methods (e.g., [25, 46]) with the addition of domain stratification, which is a fairly straightforward extension rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

VLCS noise annotations were produced by manual inspection by the authors without reported inter-annotator agreement or validation protocol, raising concerns about label reliability and reproducibility of this newly introduced "ground truth."

The paper's claims are occasionally overstated (e.g., "no existing method effectively distinguishes noise from multi-domain distributions," "a promising direction/solution") relative to the mixed and sometimes marginal empirical evidence provided.

Presentation issues: inconsistent notation/terminology between "Assumption 1" and "Theorem 1," some grammatical errors, and important method details (e.g., GMM threshold sensitivity, hyperparameter choices for the low-loss/high-loss split, computational overhead of proxy computation) are not thoroughly analyzed or ablated in the main paper.

strengths: Introduces a novel and underexplored task, Noise-Aware Generalization (NAG), that jointly considers label noise and domain shift—an intersection that prior DG and LNL literature largely treats separately.

Provides a clear and convincing motivating analysis (Fig. 1, Fig. 3, SVM support-vector experiment on RotatedMNIST) showing why naive loss/similarity-based noise detection fails when domain shift is also present.

The core idea behind DL4ND—using low-loss samples as (class, domain) proxies and leveraging cross-domain comparisons for noise detection—is intuitive, simple to integrate as a plug-and-play module, and well illustrated (Fig. 5, Fig. 6).

Extensive experimental scope: 11 SOTA DG/LNL baselines, 18 combination methods, evaluated on two real-world datasets (VLCS, CHAMMI-CP) and two synthetic noisy DG benchmarks (OfficeHome, TerraIncognita), with detailed algorithmic descriptions and implementation details in the appendix.
Valuable real-world contribution: manual noise annotation of VLCS and framing of CHAMMI-CP as a NAG benchmark, which could be useful for future work in this space.

Useful discussion/analysis section (Sec. 5.3) offering practical insights, e.g., that LNL sample selection skews domain balance, and that regularization-based LNL methods combine better with DG than sample-selection methods.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is essentially a restatement of Assumption 1 without a formal proof and adds limited theoretical rigor; it is more a motivating intuition than a rigorously established theoretical result, and the paper would benefit from either a proof or reframing it as a design hypothesis.

Results are inconsistent across datasets: on CHAMMI-CP, several DL4ND+DG variants underperform plain DG baselines on ID accuracy (e.g., SAGM+SWAD reaches 78.27 ID vs. most DL4ND combinations in the low-70s), which weakens the claim of consistent gains across 'four diverse datasets.'

No variance/error bars or multiple-seed results are reported, making it hard to judge whether reported gains (some quite small, e.g., <1% AVG improvements in several rows of Table 2) are statistically meaningful.
The manual noise annotation for VLCS is subjective and lacks inter-annotator agreement or validation, raising concerns about label-noise ground truth reliability used for evaluation and conclusions.

Key implementation details of DL4ND (e.g., how the 'optimal label update step' is chosen, sensitivity to the GMM threshold, robustness to noise ratio beyond 0.2/0.4) are only partially specified, limiting reproducibility and understanding of hyperparameter sensitivity.

The synthetic noise construction relies on manually selected 'confusing' class pairs, which is a somewhat narrow and potentially cherry-picked notion of real-world label noise, limiting generality of the synthetic evaluation.
Code is only promised to be released upon acceptance, and several writing/grammar issues throughout reduce clarity (e.g., inconsistent phrasing in the discussion and related work sections).

strengths: Well-motivated new task setting (NAG) that combines DG and LNL, with clear, concrete illustrations (Fig 1, 3) of why naive combinations of DG and LNL methods fail in this joint setting.

Extensive empirical study: 12 baseline DG/LNL methods plus ~20 combinations evaluated across 7 datasets (3 real-world, 4 synthetic noise variants) with multiple noise types (symmetric, asymmetric, dominant/real-world), giving broad coverage.

Careful diagnostic analysis (Section 3, RotatedMNIST experiments with box plots and SVM support-vector analysis) that provides intuitive and empirically grounded justification for the core design choice (using low-loss samples to build class-domain proxies before cross-domain comparison).

Thorough ablation study (Table 5) isolating the contribution of relabeling vs. removal, cross-domain vs. within-domain comparison, and small-loss vs. all-sample proxies, showing each component contributes measurable gains.
Good discussion of failure modes of naive LNL+DG combinations (e.g., UNICON skewing domain distributions, Figure 7/Table 7), which adds useful insight beyond just reporting a new SOTA number.
Reasonable reproducibility effort: code release claimed, detailed implementation/algorithm boxes in appendix for all DG+LNL combination baselines.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution (small-loss sample selection via GMM + cross-domain nearest-proxy relabeling) is an incremental extension of existing small-loss/relabeling LNL techniques (e.g., DivideMix, UNICON) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism; the main innovation is restricting proxy comparison to cross-domain groups, a relatively simple design choice.

Results are inconsistent rather than uniformly dominant: DL4ND alone sometimes underperforms DG-only or LNL-only baselines (e.g., Table 8 shows several DG methods beat DL4ND on VLCS ID/AVG), and Table 4 shows ID performance drops when DL4ND is added in some settings (e.g., ERM++ on OfficeHome, TerraIncognita), undermining the generality of the claimed gains.

The theoretical framing (Equation 2, 'formal' separability condition) is essentially descriptive/empirical rather than proven; no formal guarantee or convergence-style argument is given, and satisfaction of the condition is only checked on a single synthetic RotatedMNIST setup.

Comparison to DA+LNL literature (Appendix B) is largely qualitative/conceptual rather than an actual empirical benchmark against those specific published methods, weakening the claim that DL4ND clearly surpasses this related line of work.

Only a small number of genuinely real-world noisy multi-domain datasets are used (VLCS, CHAMMI-CP, PACS); the bulk of controlled experiments rely on synthetic asymmetric/symmetric noise injected into standard DG benchmarks, which may not faithfully represent how noise and domain shift are correlated in practice.

The one-shot (non-iterative) relabeling design is only validated on relatively small/simple benchmarks (ResNet-50/ConvNeXt scale); it is unclear how this approach scales to larger, noisier, more complex real-world settings.

The paper's writing contains multiple typos/unclear phrasings (e.g., 'ride range', 'into deeper insight', inconsistent table cross-references), suggesting the manuscript would benefit from additional proofreading and polish.

The GMM-based two-cluster split assumption for identifying low-loss vs high-loss samples is not rigorously justified for varying noise ratios or domain heterogeneity, and sensitivity to this design choice is not extensively analyzed beyond warmup-length ablations.

strengths: Introduces and clearly motivates a novel, practically relevant problem setting (Noise-Aware Generalization) at the intersection of two well-studied but rarely jointly studied areas (LNL and DG), supported by compelling illustrative examples (Figs. 1 and 3) showing why naive combinations fail.

Provides a principled analysis (Section 3) that empirically grounds the design of the proposed method, showing via RotatedMNIST experiments and SVM support-vector analysis that class/domain shifts are genuinely difficult to separate without careful proxy construction, and that this separation matters for the decision boundary.

Extensive empirical evaluation: 7 datasets (3 real-noise, 4 synthetic-noise) spanning diverse domains (web images, cell imaging, wildlife cameras), 12 DG/LNL baselines, and ~20 combination methods, giving a comprehensive picture of the NAG landscape.

Thorough ablation study (Table 5) isolating the contribution of each DL4ND component (relabeling vs. removal, cross-domain vs. same-domain comparison, low-loss vs. all-sample proxies), and a clean analysis in Section 5.2 explaining precisely why naive LNL+DG combinations underperform (domain-imbalanced relabeling).

Method is simple and lightweight (single relabeling pass using existing model features, no extra network/loss terms), which aids adoption, and reproducibility is supported via released code and detailed pseudocode for all integrated baselines in the appendix.
weaknesses: The core method relies on domain labels to construct cross-domain proxies, which the authors acknowledge as 'simplifying' the NAG challenge; this limits applicability to settings where domain labels are unavailable, somewhat undercutting the motivation that NAG should reflect realistic deployment conditions.

The central technical novelty (comparing to cross-domain rather than within-domain class proxies) is a relatively narrow modification of existing proxy-based relabeling approaches (e.g., UNICON, DISC), and the paper's formal justification (Eq. 2 and the accompanying assumption) is not proven but only empirically illustrated on a single toy dataset (RotatedMNIST).

Gains are inconsistent across settings/datasets: DL4ND alone does not always beat DG-only baselines (e.g., VLCS in Table 8), some asymmetric-noise results in Table 4 show no or marginal improvement (2 of 10 settings do not improve), and improvements on CHAMMI-CP are often small (1-2%), raising questions about robustness of the claimed benefits.

The GMM-based low-/high-loss split and reliance on 'early-learning is clean' assumptions are standard techniques already used in prior LNL literature, so this component of the pipeline is not novel; no analysis is given of failure cases where this assumption breaks down (e.g., very high noise rates, or noise concentrated in easy-to-learn domains).

No computational cost/overhead comparison is provided despite DL4ND requiring feature extraction and proxy computation across all domains and periodic warmup tuning (shown to be sensitivity-dependent in Appendix A), which is relevant for practical adoption.

Some result tables lack consistent baseline coverage (e.g., Tables 3 and 4 omit direct LNL-only comparisons that are included elsewhere), making it harder to fully judge relative standing of DL4ND against the strongest LNL alternatives in every setting.
